title: 26 U.S. Code Section 41(f) Special Rules
description: 26 U.S.C. § 41(f) treats all members of a controlled group, and all commonly controlled businesses, as a single taxpayer for the federal R&D credit.
summary: 26 U.S.C. Section 41(f) sets the special rules for the federal R&D tax credit, requiring all members of a controlled group of corporations and all commonly controlled trades or businesses to be treated as a single taxpayer. Group members combine qualified research expenses and gross receipts, disregard intercompany transactions, and share the credit in proportion to each member's qualifying expenses.

body.text: 26 U.S.C. Section 41(f) sets the special rules for the federal R&D tax credit, requiring all members of a controlled group of corporations and all commonly controlled trades or businesses to be treated as a single taxpayer. Group members combine qualified research expenses and gross receipts, disregard intercompany transactions, and share the credit in proportion to each member's qualifying expenses.

Title 26 U.S. Code Section 41(f) establishes the special aggregation, allocation, and structural rules governing the federal income tax credit for increasing research activities across commonly controlled business structures. Under the core statutory mandate of Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41(f)(1), all members of a controlled group of corporations and all trades or businesses (whether or not incorporated) under common control must be treated as a single taxpayer when computing the research and development (R&D) tax credit. This statutory consolidation prevents affiliated corporate and unincorporated entities from artificially inflating incremental research tax credits through internal restructuring, selective entity isolation, or intercompany transactions.

Modern multi-entity corporate architectures routinely separate intellectual property ownership, operational funding, commercial distribution, and physical laboratory execution across distinct domestic and foreign subsidiaries. Absent a mandatory single-taxpayer aggregation rule, a parent organization could shift qualified research expenses (QREs) or gross receipts among affiliated entities to suppress historical base amounts or concentrate incremental research spending within isolated subsidiaries, generating disproportionate tax credits without increasing actual aggregate innovation. By requiring the aggregation of all QREs and gross receipts across every entity under common control, IRC Section 41(f) ensures that the credit rewards only genuine net increases in research investment across the unified enterprise. Once the aggregate group credit is computed at the single-taxpayer level, Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-6 governs the subsequent allocation of that unified credit pool back to the individual component members in proportion to each member's contribution to the group's total QREs.

State tax jurisdictions that conform to IRC Section 41 adopt this federal single-taxpayer mandate as their structural baseline, but layer strict territorial nexus boundaries and state-specific statutory modifications over the federal computational mechanics. In jurisdictions such as California—governed by California Revenue and Taxation Code (R&TC) Section 23609 for corporate taxpayers and R&TC Section 17052.12 for personal income taxpayers—and Massachusetts—governed by Massachusetts General Laws (M.G.L.) Chapter 63, Section 38M and Department of Revenue (DOR) Regulation 830 CMR 63.38M.1 (alongside proposed regulation 830 CMR 63.38M.2)—the federal controlled group aggregation rules interact with uncompromising physical-location requirements, modified state credit percentages, diverging pass-through entity restrictions, group-level credit utilization caps, and stringent administrative and judicial substantiation standards.
The Federal Statutory and Regulatory Framework: IRC Section 41(f) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-6
Definition and Structural Scope of a Controlled Group

The operational reach of the single-taxpayer mandate rests on the statutory definition of a controlled group under IRC Section 41(f)(1) and Section 41(f)(5), which cross-references IRC Section 1563(a), Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-6(a)(3), and Treasury Regulation Section 1.52-1. Under IRC Section 41(f)(1)(A) and (B), the aggregation rules encompass both controlled groups of corporations and all trades or businesses—whether or not incorporated—that are under common control. Under Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-6(a)(3)(vi), a "trade or business" is defined as a sole proprietorship, partnership, trust, estate, or corporation carrying on a trade or business within the meaning of IRC Section 162; moreover, any corporation that is a member of a commonly controlled group is deemed to be carrying on a trade or business if any other member of that group is carrying on any trade or business. Consequently, unincorporated entities including partnerships, limited liability companies (LLCs), trusts, estates, and sole proprietorships under common control are subject to the exact same aggregation and allocation requirements as C-corporations.

Crucially, while IRC Section 1563(a) generally defines corporate control using an "at least 80 percent" ownership threshold for consolidated tax return purposes, IRC Section 41(f)(5) explicitly modifies that threshold by substituting a "more than 50 percent" ownership standard. For groups of unincorporated and incorporated trades or businesses under common control, Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-6(a)(3)(ii) incorporates the common control rules of Treasury Regulation Section 1.52-1(b) through (g) (as amended by Treasury Decision 10018, 89 FR 106851, on December 30, 2024, applicable to taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2025). Under this modified standard and Treasury Regulation Section 1.52-1, three primary organizational structures trigger mandatory controlled group aggregation.

headers: Ownership and Structural Criteria Under IRC Section 41(f) and Treas. Reg. Section 1.52-1

cells: One or more chains of organizations conducting trades or businesses connected through ownership of a controlling interest with a common parent organization, where (1) a controlling interest in each organization (except the common parent) is owned directly or via attribution (under Treas. Reg. § 1.414(c)-4(b)(1)–(3)) by one or more of the other organizations, and (2) the common parent owns a controlling interest in at least one of the other organizations, excluding direct ownership by the other organizations. Under IRC § 41(f)(5) and Treas. Reg. § 1.52-1(c)(2), a "controlling interest" means more than 50% of total combined voting power or more than 50% of total value of shares (for a corporation), more than 50% of actuarial interest (for a trust or estate), more than 50% of profit interest or capital interest (for a partnership), or ownership of a sole proprietorship.

Two or more organizations conducting trades or businesses owned by five or fewer persons (individuals, estates, or trusts). Under IRC § 1563(a)(2) for corporate groups, those five or fewer persons must possess more than 50% of the total combined voting power or more than 50% of the total value of shares of each corporation, taking into account each person's ownership only to the extent such ownership is identical across each organization. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.52-1(d) for trades or businesses under common control, the same five or fewer persons must satisfy both (1) the effective control test (more than 50% identical ownership across each organization in voting power/value, actuarial interest, or profit/capital interest) and (2) the controlling interest test (at least 80% aggregate ownership of voting power/value for a corporation, actuarial interest for a trust/estate, or profit/capital interest for a partnership).

Three or more organizations in which (1) each organization is a member of either a parent-subsidiary group under common control or a brother-sister group under common control, and (2) at least one organization is both the common parent organization of a parent-subsidiary group under common control and a member of a brother-sister group under common control.

body.text: Under Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-6(a)(1) and Section 1.41-6(g), control status and a member's allowable credit are evaluated as of the close of the taxable year—specifically December 31 for calendar-year taxpayers. When controlled group members have different tax accounting periods, the computing member treats the taxable year of another member ending with or within the computing member's credit year as that member's credit year. Under Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-6(h), a business can be a member of only one group per taxable year; if eligible for membership in multiple groups, it is included in the group to which it belonged in the preceding taxable year or must designate its group on a timely filed return.

In administrative enforcement practice, the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) Audit Techniques Guide (ATG) for the Credit for Increasing Research Activities (IRC Section 41) directs examining agents to verify at the outset of an examination whether the taxpayer belongs to a controlled group and whether all required domestic and foreign affiliates have been included in the aggregate computation, identifying incomplete controlled group aggregation as a recurring cause of audit adjustments. Specifically, the IRS ATG mandates that the gross receipts of all entities required to aggregate their expenditures under IRC Section 41(f)(1)(A) and (B) must be included in the aggregate gross receipts computation, regardless of whether the individual affiliated entities incurred any QREs of their own. The IRS ATG also highlights IRC Section 41(f)(3), which requires adjustments to the historical base amount when a major portion of a trade or business is acquired or disposed of, while noting that bare stock acquisitions or dispositions standing alone do not trigger Section 41(f)(3) trade or business adjustments.
Mechanics of Aggregation and Uniform Election Requirements

Under Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-6(b)(1), computing the group credit requires treating all controlled group members universally as a single taxpayer and applying all Section 41 computational rules on an aggregate basis. Every member's current-year QREs, historical QREs, and gross receipts must be combined into a single computational pool as though the disparate legal entities constituted a single corporation. This single-taxpayer treatment also governs start-up company status under Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-6(b)(2): a controlled group is treated as a start-up company under IRC Section 41(c)(3)(B)(i) only if there was no taxable year beginning before January 1, 1984, in which a member of the group had gross receipts while the same or another member had QREs, or if there were fewer than three taxable years beginning after December 31, 1983, and before January 1, 1989, in which a member had gross receipts while the same or another member had QREs.

This single-taxpayer consolidation neutralizes intercompany transactions for research credit purposes under Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-6(b) and the specific intra-group transaction rules of Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-6(i). Under Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-6(i)(1) and (2), if Member A of a controlled group contracts with and pays Member B of the same group to perform research activities, the financial transfer between Member A and Member B is disregarded in the group credit calculation. The member performing qualified research on behalf of another member includes its in-house research expenses in its QREs and does not treat the intercompany payments received as disqualifying funded research, while the paying member cannot claim those intercompany payments as contract research expenses. Only the underlying wages, supply costs, and eligible third-party expenses actually incurred by the performing member are counted, preventing the double-counting of a single research expenditure as both contract research for the payor and in-house research for the performer. Furthermore, under Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-6(i)(3) and (4), contract research expenses paid to outside third parties are included by the paying member (or by another group member that reimburses the payor and carries on a related trade or business if paid outside the payor's trade or business), intra-group payments for supplies are capped at the lesser of the amount paid or the selling member's tax basis in the supplies, internal lease payments for personal property owned by a group member are disregarded, and intra-group lease payments for property leased from outside parties are capped at the lesser of the intra-group payment or the actual external lease cost.

Furthermore, Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-6(b)(1) and Section 1.41-9(b)(2) enforce strict methodological uniformity across the controlled group for any given taxable year. All members of the controlled group must compute the credit using the exact same calculation regime: a group cannot permit one subsidiary to apply the Regular Research Credit (RRC) methodology under IRC Section 41(a)(1) while another subsidiary applies the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) methodology under IRC Section 41(c)(4) (formerly numbered IRC Section 41(c)(5) prior to the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2018, Pub. L. 115-141). Under Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-9(b)(2) and the instructions to IRS Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities), an ASC election—or revocation thereof—is made on the return of the controlled group's "designated member" (defined as the member of the group that is allocated the greatest amount of the group credit under Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-6(c)) and binds the entire controlled group.
Legislative Evolution of Credit Allocation: The American Taxpayer Relief Act of 2012

The statutory mechanism for allocating the aggregated group credit back to individual controlled group members underwent a structural overhaul with the enactment of Section 301(c) of the American Taxpayer Relief Act of 2012 (ATRA), Public Law 112-240 (H.R. 8).

Prior to the ATRA amendments, former Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-6(c) required a two-tier allocation methodology anchored on a "stand-alone entity credit" calculation. Under that pre-ATRA framework, each member of the controlled group had to compute what its hypothetical research credit would have been on an independent, stand-alone basis if the single-taxpayer rule did not exist. The aggregate group credit was first allocated in proportion to each member's stand-alone entity credit; only if the total group credit exceeded the sum of all members' stand-alone credits was the residual excess allocated according to relative QRE shares.

In practice, the pre-ATRA stand-alone allocation regime created severe economic distortions within diversified corporate groups. A research-intensive subsidiary could incur substantial current-year QREs that drove the majority of the controlled group's aggregate credit, yet possess a high historical fixed-base percentage or elevated stand-alone gross receipts that caused its hypothetical stand-alone credit calculation to equal zero. Under the pre-ATRA regulation, such an operating subsidiary received zero allocation of the group credit unless the group credit exceeded the sum of all other members' stand-alone credits, diverting the tax benefit to sister entities with lower incremental research investment.

Section 301(c) of ATRA eliminated this distortion by amending IRC Section 41(f)(1)(A)(ii) and Section 41(f)(1)(B)(ii) to abolish the stand-alone entity credit calculation altogether. Under the post-ATRA statutory mandate—implemented via final and temporary regulations published on April 3, 2015, in Treasury Decision (T.D.) 9717 (80 FR 18096; corrected April 27, 2015, at 80 FR 23237 and 80 FR 23238; cross-referencing notice of proposed rulemaking REG-133489-13, 80 FR 18171) and finalized without change by the Treasury Department on March 28, 2018, in Treasury Decision (T.D.) 9832 (83 FR 13185, effective April 2, 2018, modifying Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-6(c) and (d), updating cross-references in Section 1.45G-1(f) and Section 1.280C-4(b)(2), and removing temporary regulations Section 1.41-6T, Section 1.45G-1T, and Section 1.280C-4T)—the aggregate group credit is allocated to each member strictly in proportion to that member's share of the controlled group's aggregate QREs, basic research payments, and amounts paid or incurred to energy research consortiums for the credit year, irrespective of what any member's stand-alone base amount or stand-alone credit would have been.
Treatment of Consolidated Return Groups Within Larger Controlled Groups

Additional allocation rules apply when a controlled group contains a subset of corporations that file a consolidated federal income tax return (as defined in Treasury Regulation Section 1.1502-1(h)) alongside other commonly controlled entities, such as unincorporated partnerships, LLCs, or non-consolidated corporations. Under Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-6(d)(1), all members of a consolidated group who are members of a controlled group are treated collectively as a single member of the broader controlled group during the primary credit allocation step.

First, the overarching controlled group allocates a single block of the group credit to the consolidated group based on the ratio of the consolidated group's combined QREs to the entire controlled group's aggregate QREs. Second, under Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-6(d)(3), that allocated block of credit is sub-allocated among the individual corporate members of the consolidated return group strictly in proportion to each consolidated member's QREs relative to the consolidated group's total aggregate QREs. As illustrated in Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-6(e) (Example 2), if controlled group members D ($240x QREs), E ($360x QREs), and consolidated group FGH ($600x combined QREs across F's $120x, G's $240x, and H's $240x) generate a $100x group credit on $1,200x of total group QREs, the primary step allocates $20x to D, $30x to E, and $50x to consolidated group FGH; the secondary step then sub-allocates FGH's $50x credit as $10x to F ($120x / $600x), $20x to G ($240x / $600x), and $20x to H ($240x / $600x). This two-tier waterfall preserves alignment between tax credit ownership and the specific legal entities bearing the financial risk and expense of research.
Federal Judicial Interpretation: Procter & Gamble Co. v. United States

The application of IRC Section 41(f)'s single-taxpayer mandate to multinational controlled groups was tested in the federal district court litigation Procter & Gamble Co. v. United States, 733 F. Supp. 2d 857, No. 1:08-cv-00608 (TSB) (S.D. Ohio July 6, 2010) (decided by U.S. District Judge Timothy S. Black). Because the base amount under the Regular Research Credit methodology (IRC Section 41(c)(1)) is directly proportional to the taxpayer's average annual gross receipts over the four preceding taxable years, any expansion of the "gross receipts" denominator directly inflates the base amount and reduces the resulting research credit.

During the IRS audit of Procter & Gamble's 2001 through 2005 tax years, the IRS contended that intercompany sales and licensing receipts received by domestic controlled group members from foreign subsidiaries (controlled foreign corporations, or CFCs) within the same controlled group had to be included in the domestic group's gross receipts calculation. Including those foreign intercompany receipts substantially increased Procter & Gamble's base amount, prompting the IRS to seek the disallowance of claimed federal research tax credits.

The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Ohio granted Procter & Gamble's motion for partial summary judgment and denied the government's cross-motion, holding that the taxpayer properly excluded receipts derived from transactions with its foreign controlled group subsidiaries. Analyzing IRC Section 41(f)(1)(A)(i) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-6(i) (then § 1.41-6T(i)), the court concluded that IRC Section 41(f) is unambiguous: because all members of the same controlled group must be treated as a single taxpayer, transfers and financial transactions between controlled group members cannot generate gross receipts, as a single taxpayer cannot generate gross receipts from transactions with itself, and including international intercompany transactions would double-count gross receipts. Following the 2010 decision in Procter & Gamble, the IRS ceased contesting the exclusion of intercompany gross receipts from CFCs in computing the base amount, formally conceding the issue on partial summary judgment in Hewlett-Packard Co. v. Commissioner, 139 T.C. No. 8 (2012).
California State Framework and Statutory Modifications (R&TC Section 23609)

California incorporates the federal research credit structure of IRC Section 41—including the controlled group aggregation rules of IRC Section 41(f)—through California Revenue and Taxation Code (R&TC) Section 23609 under the Corporation Tax Law and R&TC Section 17052.12 under the Personal Income Tax Law. While the federal research credit historically required periodic congressional extensions prior to becoming permanent, the California R&D tax credit operates as a permanent feature of the state's tax code, albeit with sovereign statutory modifications that substantially alter the credit's territorial scope, rates, election procedures, and utilization.
The Strict Geographic Limitation Requirement

The primary structural divergence between federal IRC Section 41 and California R&TC Section 23609 is California's strict territorial nexus mandate. Whereas federal law permits QREs for research conducted anywhere within the United States (or Puerto Rico and U.S. possessions under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(F)), R&TC Section 23609(c)(2) (and R&TC Section 17052.12(f)) modifies the federal definition so that "qualified research" and "basic research" encompass exclusively research activities physically conducted within the geographic borders of California. Additionally, California modifies IRC Section 41(b)(1) under R&TC Section 23609(c)(1) to exclude from QREs amounts paid for tangible personal property qualifying for the sales and use tax exemption under R&TC Section 6378, decouples from IRC Section 41(b)(3)(D) (amounts paid to eligible small businesses, universities, and federal laboratories) and IRC Section 41(f)(6) (energy research consortiums) under R&TC Section 23609(m) and (n) (as renumbered by Senate Bill 711 in 2025), and treats 75 percent (instead of the standard 65 percent) of payments made to certain nonprofit qualified research consortia under IRC Section 41(b)(3)(C) as QREs under R&TC Section 23609(g).

For a multi-state controlled group subject to IRC Section 41(f) aggregation, this geographic boundary requires a bifurcated accounting architecture. When computing the California group credit, the controlled group must strip out all non-California activities from its federal QRE pool, isolating solely qualified wages paid for services physically performed by employees within California, non-depreciable tangible supplies physically used or consumed in California-based laboratories or research facilities, and contract research payments for research activities physically performed at facilities located inside California. Activities conducted in other jurisdictions such as Nevada, Oregon, or Canada fail the California territorial requirement even when funded, directed, supervised, or commercially exploited by a California-headquartered parent corporation. All such out-of-state expenditures and out-of-state gross receipts must be excluded from the California controlled group's computation.
Qualification Standards: The Mandatory Four-Part Test

To qualify for inclusion in the California controlled group computation, research activities physically performed in California must satisfy the four-part statutory qualification test of IRC Section 41(d), as enforced by the California Franchise Tax Board (FTB) and the California Office of Tax Appeals (OTA).

cells: Expenditures connected with the activity must be eligible for treatment as specified research or experimental expenditures under IRC § 174, and the research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information whose application is intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component (defined as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used in the taxpayer's trade or business).

The process of discovering information must fundamentally rely on principles of the "hard sciences," specifically the physical sciences, biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. Activities grounded in social sciences, arts, humanities, economics, or market research are statutorily excluded.

At the outset of the activity, the taxpayer must intend to discover information that would eliminate technical uncertainty concerning the capability or method for developing or improving the business component, or the appropriate design of that business component.

Substantially all—defined quantitatively under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) as 80% or more—of the research activities for each business component measured on a cost or time basis must constitute elements of a process of experimentation relating to a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality (and not style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design features under IRC § 41(d)(3)(B)). The taxpayer must identify technical alternatives and systematically evaluate one or more of those alternatives through modeling, simulation, systematic trial and error, or the scientific method.

body.text: California Calculation Methodologies and Statutory Rates

California modifies the federal computational rates and historical base formulas under R&TC Section 23609 and Section 17052.12 to reflect state fiscal priorities, rewarding both incremental corporate research spending and university-based foundational inquiry. Under the California Regular Research Credit (RRC), the state reduces the federal 20 percent regular credit rate to 15 percent of current-year California QREs that exceed a computed California base amount (R&TC Section 23609(b)). That base amount equals the product of the taxpayer's fixed-base percentage and the average annual California gross receipts for the four preceding taxable years. For established taxpayers, the fixed-base percentage is derived from the ratio of aggregate California QREs to aggregate California gross receipts during the 1984–1988 base period (subject to a statutory maximum fixed-base percentage of 16 percent under IRC Section 41(c)(3)(C)), whereas newer taxpayers apply statutory start-up formulas under IRC Section 41(c)(3)(B) (beginning at 3 percent for the first five post-1993 QRE years). In conformity with IRC Section 41(c)(2), the California base amount is subject to the statutory 50 percent minimum base floor, ensuring that the base amount cannot be less than 50 percent of current-year California QREs. Under R&TC Section 23609(i) (renumbered from R&TC Section 23609(h)(3) by SB 711 in 2025) and R&TC Section 17052.12(h) (renumbered from Section 17052.12(g)(3)), California modifies "gross receipts" under IRC Section 41(c)(6) to include only gross receipts from the sale of property held for sale in the ordinary course of business that is delivered or shipped to a purchaser within California, regardless of free on board (f.o.b.) point or other conditions of sale.

Alongside the regular credit, California provides an enhanced Basic Research Credit (BRC) for corporations under R&TC Section 23609(c)(2) and (d) equal to 24 percent of Basic Research Payments (BRPs) made to Qualified Organizations (QOs). This 24 percent corporate rate exceeds the federal 20 percent equivalent and reflects a deliberate state policy to channel corporate research funding into California universities, higher education institutions, and tax-exempt scientific research organizations. To qualify for the 24 percent BRC rate, payments must be made by a corporation in cash pursuant to a written contract, and the underlying foundational scientific inquiry must take place entirely within California.

Historically, for taxable years beginning before January 1, 2025, California diverged from federal law by declining to conform to the federal Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC), instead requiring taxpayers that elected out of the Regular Research Credit to use the three-tier Alternative Incremental Credit (AIC / AIRC) under former R&TC Section 23609(h)(1) and Section 17052.12(g)(1), which applied tiered rates of 1.49 percent (for California QREs exceeding 1 percent up to 1.5 percent of four-year average California gross receipts), 1.98 percent (exceeding 1.5 percent up to 2 percent), and 2.48 percent (exceeding 2 percent). However, pursuant to Senate Bill 711 (SB 711, Chapter 231, Statutes of 2025, chaptered October 1, 2025)—which updated California's general IRC conformity specified date from January 2015 to January 1, 2025—for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2025, California explicitly repealed the AIC and formally conformed to the federal ASC structure under IRC Section 41(c)(4) with California-specific rate modifications codified at R&TC Section 23609(h)(2)(A) and R&TC Section 17052.12(g)(2)(A).

Under the SB 711 regime, the standard California ASC equals 3 percent (modifying the 14 percent federal rate in IRC Section 41(c)(4)(A)) of current-year California QREs that exceed 50 percent of the average California QREs for the three preceding taxable years (R&TC Section 23609(h)(2)(A) and Section 17052.12(g)(2)(A)(i)). If the taxpayer incurred no California QREs in any one of the three preceding taxable years, a start-up / zero-prior-QRE ASC rate of 1.3 percent (modifying the 6 percent federal rate in IRC Section 41(c)(4)(B)(ii)) applies to current-year California QREs (R&TC Section 23609(h)(2)(A) and Section 17052.12(g)(2)(A)(ii)). Taxpayers who previously elected the repealed AIC do not default to either the Regular credit or the ASC; controlled groups and taxpayers claiming the California credit must make an affirmative, binding election between the Regular method and the ASC method on a timely filed original return using Form FTB 3523 (Research Credit). Under R&TC Section 23609(h)(2)(B) and Section 17052.12(g)(2)(B), IRC Section 41(c)(4)(C) does not apply in California, meaning "deemed consent" to revoke an ASC election does not apply; once made, an election to use the ASC cannot be revoked in subsequent years unless the taxpayer requests and receives formal written consent from the FTB prior to filing the timely filed original return for the taxable year (by submitting federal Form 3115 or Form 1128 to the FTB Change in Accounting Periods and Methods Coordinator in accordance with FTB Notice 2024-01).
Temporary Credit Utilization Caps and Pass-Through Entity Mechanics

Although unused California R&D tax credits carry forward indefinitely until exhausted (and cannot be carried back), state budget legislation enacted in 2024—specifically Senate Bill 167 (SB 167) and Senate Bill 175 (SB 175, Chapter 42, Statutes of 2024), codified at R&TC Section 23036.4 (Corporation Tax Law) and R&TC Section 17039.4 (Personal Income Tax Law)—enacted a temporary business credit utilization limitation for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2024, and before January 1, 2027. During this three-year window, business tax credits—including current and carryforward R&D credits—cannot reduce net tax (for personal income filers) or tax (for corporate filers) by more than $5,000,000 per taxable year. Crucially for multi-entity structures, under R&TC Section 23036.4 and the Form FTB 3523 Instructions, where taxpayers are included in a unitary combined report, this $5,000,000 annual utilization cap is enforced strictly at the aggregate group level, rather than on a separate per-entity basis, preventing combined reporting groups from multiplying the $5,000,000 cap across affiliated subsidiaries. Under SB 175 and the Form FTB 3523 Instructions, taxpayers (other than S-corporations with respect to entity-level credits) may make an annual, irrevocable all-or-nothing election on Form FTB 3870 attached to an original, timely filed return to receive an annual refundable credit for business credits disallowed specifically due to the $5,000,000 limitation, claimed at 20 percent per year over a five-year refundable period beginning in the third taxable year after the election year; if no refundable election is made, the carryover period for disallowed credits is extended by the number of taxable years the credit was disallowed.

For pass-through entities (partnerships, LLCs classified as partnerships, and S-corporations) operating within a controlled group, the allocated group credit is computed on Form FTB 3523 and reported to partners, members, or shareholders on Schedule K-1. Under R&TC Section 23803(a)(1) and the Form FTB 3523 Instructions, California applies a dual-application framework to S-corporations under which the corporate entity itself is permitted to claim one-third (1/3) of the generated research credit on Schedule C (100S) against its 1.5 percent entity-level franchise or income tax (or 3.5 percent entity-level tax for financial S-corporations), while 100 percent of the generated research credit simultaneously passes through on a pro-rata basis to the S-corporation's individual shareholders via Schedule K-1 (100S) to offset their California personal income tax liabilities (subject to the 98.5 percent (.985) shareholder credit reduction percentage if the S-corporation reports the credit without the IRC Section 280C(c) reduction, while any prior C-corporation credit carryovers held when electing S-corporation status are reduced to 1/3 and locked at the entity level with the remaining 2/3 disregarded).
State Executive Branch Enforcement and Administrative Guidance

The California Franchise Tax Board (FTB) administers and enforces R&TC Section 23609 and Section 17052.12. Following the legislative sunset of earlier California corporate tax incentives—specifically the Manufacturers' Investment Credit (MIC) and the Enterprise Zone credit regime—the FTB reassigned specialized examination personnel to dedicated R&D tax credit audit teams, producing a significant increase in research credit audit activity.
FTB Audit Posture and Examination Priorities

FTB specialist examination teams concentrate audit enforcement on three primary technical fronts. First, although FTB Chief Counsel statements (including November 2013 statements by FTB Chief Counsel Jozel Brunett, December 2013 FTB Tax News, and March 2014 confirmation by FTB Tax Counsel Kristin Kane) indicate that the FTB generally follows federal IRS determinations where California law conforms to federal law, the FTB is not bound by an IRS audit acceptance or settlement and initiates independent technical re-examinations of QRE claims whenever FTB auditors conclude that the IRS did not apply sufficient scrutiny to project qualification or cost substantiation. Second, FTB examiners intensely audit payroll records, employee location logs, travel vouchers, and supply invoices to verify geographic nexus under R&TC Section 23609(c)(2) and ensure that no out-of-state wages, travel costs, or out-of-state supply consumption are improperly embedded within the California QRE calculation. Third, because the 24 percent Basic Research Credit under R&TC Section 23609(d) carries California's highest statutory rate, FTB auditors closely inspect written contracts between corporate payors and Qualified Organizations to confirm that corporate payments fund specific, contracted foundational research physically conducted in California rather than unrestricted philanthropic grants or general university donations. Additionally, under the California Supreme Court's decision in General Motors Corp. v. FTB, research credits allocated to a member of a unitary combined reporting group can only be used to offset the tax liability of the specific corporate member that generated/received the allocated credit, and cannot be shared across other members of the unitary group (requiring entity-by-entity tracking in Part III of Form FTB 3523).
FTB Legal Division Guidance 2012-03-01

A recurring interpretive issue for controlled groups involves pre-revenue start-up subsidiaries (such as early-stage biotechnology or software entities) or purely service companies that incur substantial California QREs but have zero "gross receipts" within the meaning of former R&TC Section 23609(h)(3) (renumbered to R&TC Section 23609(i) by SB 711 in 2025, which defines California gross receipts solely as sales of tangible property delivered or shipped to a purchaser in California). In June 2011, the FTB initially issued Legal Division Guidance 2011-06-01 advising that a purely service company with no "gross receipts" within the meaning of R&TC Section 23609(h)(3) could not claim the California R&D credit, before withdrawing Guidance 2011-06-01 in July 2011. On March 16, 2012, in FTB Legal Division Guidance 2012-03-01, the FTB officially reversed its initial position and confirmed that a taxpayer with zero "gross receipts" within the meaning of R&TC Section 23609(h)(3) (now R&TC Section 23609(i)) remains legally eligible to claim the California R&D credit. Consequently, pre-revenue or service entities operating standalone or within a controlled group are not disqualified by the absence of California gross receipts and may compute the credit using the Regular credit base rules (subject to the 50 percent minimum base floor) or the post-2024 California ASC methodology (which the 2025 Form FTB 3523 Instructions specifically advise taxpayers with no California gross receipts under R&TC Section 17052.12(h) or Section 23609(i) to elect).
California Administrative and Judicial Case Law: Office of Tax Appeals (OTA) Precedents

Disputes arising from FTB denials of research credit claims under R&TC Section 23609 and Section 17052.12 are adjudicated by the California Office of Tax Appeals (OTA). Recent precedential and non-precedential OTA opinions establish stringent evidentiary and methodological requirements for taxpayers and controlled groups.
Evidentiary Burden and Granular Substantiation: Appeal of First Solar, Inc.

In the precedential opinion Appeal of First Solar, Inc., 2023-OTA-532P (decided September 19, 2023; made precedential November 2023; OTA Case No. 21088511), the OTA defined the standard of proof required to substantiate California R&D credit claims. First Solar, a solar technology manufacturer operating within a multi-entity structure, acquired a company that had activities in both California and Canada and reportedly had over $2,000,000 in R&D credit carryforwards, which First Solar claimed on its 2013 California return. First Solar sought to substantiate its claimed research expenses by submitting four items of evidence: (1) audited financial statements containing an aggregate line item for R&D expenses without underlying audit working papers or itemization of specific expenses; (2) a list of 15 patent applications submitted by the taxpayer; (3) documents relating to a prior-year IRS audit that did not show the IRS had examined the R&D credit; and (4) oral testimony by the company's co-founder and Chief Technology Officer.

The OTA sustained the FTB's disallowance in full, holding that summary audited financial statements, high-level accounting totals, lists of patent applications, unexamined prior IRS audit records, and generalized witness testimony are legally insufficient to satisfy the taxpayer's burden of proof. Specifically, the OTA concluded that the evidence as a whole failed to establish either that substantially all of the research activities constituted a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose, or which specific expenses were incurred in California versus in Canada. To substantiate a claim under R&TC Section 23609, a taxpayer must produce detailed, contemporaneous working papers that itemize the exact underlying expenditures and logically link specific California employee wages and supply costs to specific qualified research projects. Similarly, in the companion non-precedential opinion Appeal of Electronic Data Systems Corporation & Subsidiaries, 2023-OTA-540 (September 20, 2023), the OTA rejected a taxpayer's reliance on post-hoc employee surveys created after the research activities had already been completed, noting that the surveys lacked contemporaneous supporting documentation, were filled out by employees without relevant legal experience or evidence of impartiality, and were not signed under penalty of perjury. Within a controlled group, First Solar and Electronic Data Systems render high-level cost-center estimates or post-hoc entity-level allocations indefensible on appeal.
Application of the Process of Experimentation Test: Appeal of Abramson

In the non-precedential opinion Appeal of Abramson, et al., 2024-OTA-636 (Opinion on Petition for Rehearing issued October 9, 2024, denying rehearing of the original Opinion issued December 14, 2023; OTA Case Nos. 21067893, 21118984, & 21119139), the OTA addressed the application of the "substantially all" (80 percent) threshold under the Process of Experimentation test. The taxpayers, partners in the architectural firm Abramson Teiger Architects, LLP (ATA), claimed pass-through R&D credits for tax years 2013 through 2017 and contended that because they selectively included only the specific employee hours dedicated to active experimentation in their QRE claim, 100 percent of their claimed hours inherently satisfied the 80 percent Process of Experimentation threshold.

The OTA rejected this circular methodology and affirmed the FTB's denial. The tribunal held that the 80 percent "substantially all" requirement of IRC Section 41(d)(1)(C) must be evaluated across all research activities performed on each "business component" as a whole, rather than by cherry-picking isolated experimental hours from a broader development project. Citing Appeal of First Solar, Inc., 2023-OTA-532P, the OTA found that the taxpayers' timesheet entries (which contained vague descriptions such as "design meeting" and "go through keynotes for plans") and oral testimony failed to substantiate the precise activities constituting a process of experimentation. Furthermore, the OTA held that because the taxpayers lacked detailed contemporaneous records segregating sub-component activities and time spent on specific sub-activities, the tribunal could not apply the "shrinking-back rule" of Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(b)(2)—which otherwise allows a taxpayer to narrow the definition of a business component to a smaller subset or sub-component when the overall product fails the four-part test—and reiterated that California does not conform to federal burden-shifting under IRC Section 7491.
Distinguishing Hard Science and Scientific Experimentation from Aesthetic Design: Appeals of Swat-Fame, Inc., et al.

In the precedential decisions Appeals of Swat-Fame, Inc., et al., 2020-OTA-046P (Precedential Opinion on the Merits issued March 22, 2019; revised June 1, 2020; OTA Case Nos. 18010702, 18012114, & 18012115) and Appeals of Swat-Fame, Inc., et al., 2020-OTA-045P (Precedential Opinion on Petition for Rehearing issued March 3, 2020; revised June 1, 2020), an S-corporation apparel designer and manufacturer and its shareholders claimed approximately $2.46 million in aggregate California R&D tax credit refunds and carryover assessments across tax years 2008 through 2012 for garment design, CAD pattern creation, fabric selection, fit testing, and wash/shrinkage adjustments examined across four sample projects (Bermuda shorts, a spaghetti-strap slip dress, a ruffle skirt and legging set, and a sundress and shrug).

The OTA ruled in favor of the FTB and disallowed the claimed credits in full, holding that the taxpayers failed to demonstrate that substantially all (80 percent or more) of their activities for any of the four sample projects constituted elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose under R&TC Section 23609 and IRC Section 41(d)(1)(C) and (d)(3)(B). Relying on Union Carbide Corp. & Subsidiaries v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2009-50, aff'd, 697 F.3d 104 (2d Cir. 2012), the OTA held that a qualifying process of experimentation requires a structured, methodical plan in the "scientific method sense" (testing a hypothesis, analyzing data, refining, and retesting) rather than simple trial-and-error, applying standard industry solutions (such as adding a lining or bar-tack stitching), or evaluating style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design features disqualified under IRC Section 41(d)(3)(B). Because the taxpayers failed the Process of Experimentation test and lacked evidence to apply the shrinking-back rule under Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(b)(2), the OTA denied the claims in their entirety.

cells: Sufficiency of audited financial statements, patent lists, prior IRS audit documents, and witness testimony to substantiate QREs.

Denied: Summary accounting totals, patent application lists, and testimony do not prove QRE eligibility or California nexus (CA vs. Canada); taxpayers must provide granular working papers linking specific wages and supplies to specific qualified projects.
Appeal of Electronic Data Systems Corp. & Subsidiaries
Sufficiency of post-hoc employee surveys created after research concluded to substantiate QREs.
Denied: Retrospective employee surveys lacking contemporaneous documentation, legal training, impartiality, or statements under penalty of perjury fail to substantiate QRE claims.
2024-OTA-636 (Non-precedential PFR Opinion; Oct. 9, 2024; Original Opinion Dec. 14, 2023)
Whether claiming only experimental hours satisfies the 80% "substantially all" Process of Experimentation threshold.

Denied: The 80% threshold applies to each business component as a whole, not isolated hours; detailed contemporaneous project records are required to invoke the shrinking-back rule under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2).
2020-OTA-046P (Precedential Merits Opinion; Mar. 22, 2019) / 2020-OTA-045P (Precedential PFR Opinion; Mar. 3, 2020)
Qualification of garment design, fit-testing, and wash activities under the Process of Experimentation and Qualified Purpose tests.

Denied: Disallowed ~$2.46M in claims; routine trial-and-error and activities driven by aesthetic, style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors fail the scientific experimentation and qualified purpose requirements of R&TC § 23609.

body.text: Comparative State Framework: The Massachusetts Approach (M.G.L. c. 63, Section 38M)

Comparing California's regime with the Massachusetts Research Credit under M.G.L. Chapter 63, Section 38M and Massachusetts Department of Revenue (DOR) Regulation 830 CMR 63.38M.1 (as well as proposed regulation 830 CMR 63.38M.2, dated May 26, 2016, applying to tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2015, where the Modified General Method provides 10 percent of excess Massachusetts QREs plus 15 percent of basic research payments alongside a phased-in Massachusetts Alternative Simplified Method reaching 10 percent for calendar years beginning on or after January 1, 2021, or 5 percent if no Massachusetts QREs were incurred in any of the three preceding years) illustrates how another major innovation jurisdiction adapts the federal controlled group rules of IRC Section 41(f).
Controlled Group Aggregation and Physical Apportionment in Massachusetts

Like California, Massachusetts enforces the single-taxpayer mandate for controlled groups. Under 830 CMR 63.38M.1(7) (and proposed 830 CMR 63.38M.2), two or more corporations or entities that are members of the same controlled group within the meaning of IRC Section 41(f)(5) or under common control under Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-6(a)(3)(ii)—regardless of whether all members are actually doing business or subject to tax in Massachusetts—must aggregate their qualified research activities as an "aggregated group" to compute the Massachusetts research credit. All members of an aggregated group must compute gross receipts in the same manner (an election to use Massachusetts gross receipts binds all members for a three-year period under 830 CMR 63.38M.1(7)(b)), are subject to a 50 percent minimum aggregated base amount floor, and allocate the aggregated credit to each member corporation doing business in Massachusetts based on the ratio of that member's Massachusetts QREs and basic research payments to the total Massachusetts QREs and basic research payments of all members.

Simultaneously, Massachusetts enforces a strict physical location boundary under 830 CMR 63.38M.1(4) (and proposed 830 CMR 63.38M.2), requiring that eligible research expenses meet IRC Section 41(b) requirements and be incurred for research activity conducted physically within the Commonwealth of Massachusetts. For controlled groups with mobile employees or distributed computing infrastructure, Massachusetts DOR regulations mandate granular physical apportionment across both personnel wages and leased computing hardware. Specifically, under 830 CMR 63.38M.1(4)(b)1–2, if a research engineer divides working hours between a laboratory in Boston, Massachusetts, and an office in New York, only the precise fraction of wages attributable to qualified services ("direct research," "direct supervision," or "direct support" under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(B)) physically performed inside Massachusetts—and supplies used or consumed in Massachusetts—qualifies as a Massachusetts QRE. Similarly, under 830 CMR 63.38M.1(4)(b)3, for computer fees to qualify as in-house research expenses under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(A)(iii), the payments must be for the right to use computers physically located in Massachusetts in the conduct of qualified research taking place in Massachusetts.
Entity-Level Restrictions for S-Corporations in Massachusetts

Whereas California permits S-corporations to pass through 100 percent of their generated research credit to individual shareholders (alongside the one-third entity-level offset), Massachusetts imposes a strict entity-level lock on S-corporation research credits. Under 830 CMR 63.38M.1(3)(e) (and proposed 830 CMR 63.38M.2), an S-corporation may apply the Massachusetts research credit solely at the corporate entity level to offset its own corporate excise tax liability under either the non-income measure or, if applicable, the income measure of the corporate excise. None of the Massachusetts research credit flows through to the S-corporation's individual shareholders to offset their personal income tax liabilities. (Under proposed 830 CMR 63.38M.2, however, credit generated by an unincorporated entity or non-Massachusetts corporation in an aggregated group that is allocated to a Massachusetts-taxable corporate member is deemed generated by that Massachusetts corporation for carryover purposes.)

Furthermore, under M.G.L. Chapter 63, Section 38M and 830 CMR 63.38M.1(8), Massachusetts caps annual credit utilization: the research credit may offset up to 100 percent of the first $25,000 of corporate excise tax liability (which must be apportioned across members of an aggregated group under 830 CMR 63.38M.1(8)(a)2), but is restricted to 75 percent of any corporate excise tax liability exceeding $25,000. Any credit amounts disallowed as a result of this 75 percent excise cap may be carried forward indefinitely, whereas other unused credits exceeding total tax liability may be carried forward for 15 years (and unused credits may be shared with other Massachusetts combined group members under 830 CMR 63.38M.1(8) and 830 CMR 63.32B.2(9), though carryovers are retained by the member that generated the credit).
Worked Hypothetical Example: Multi-State Controlled Group Computation Under California Law (2025 Tax Year)

To demonstrate the operational mechanics of IRC Section 41(f) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-6 interacting with California R&TC Section 23609 and the Senate Bill 711 ASC regime, consider a hypothetical controlled group computation for the 2025 taxable year.
Hypothetical Controlled Group Profile and Step-by-Step Recomputation

Assume Innovation Holdings Inc. is a parent corporation that owns 100 percent of two operating subsidiaries: CaliTech LLC and Nevada Ops LLC. Because Innovation Holdings Inc. owns more than 50 percent of both subsidiaries, all three entities form a parent-subsidiary controlled group under IRC Section 41(f)(5), Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-6, and Treasury Regulation Section 1.52-1(c), and must be treated as a single taxpayer. During the 2025 taxable year, Innovation Holdings Inc. operates in San Jose, California, incurring $400,000 in California QREs and generating $2,000,000 in California gross receipts. CaliTech LLC operates in San Francisco, California, incurring $600,000 in California QREs and generating $3,000,000 in California gross receipts. Meanwhile, Nevada Ops LLC operates exclusively in Reno, Nevada, incurring $500,000 in Nevada QREs and generating $4,000,000 in Nevada gross receipts. Assume further that the controlled group's aggregate California QREs for the three preceding taxable years (2022–2024) averaged $800,000 per year.

items: Step 1 — Geographic Nexus Filtering and Intercompany Elimination: The controlled group must apply California's geographic nexus filter under R&TC Section 23609(c)(2) and eliminate intercompany transactions under Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-6(b) and (i). Because research conducted outside California is statutorily excluded from the California calculation, Nevada Ops LLC's $500,000 in Nevada QREs and $4,000,000 in Nevada gross receipts are excluded in full (reducing the $1,500,000 total federal QRE pool to $1,000,000 in eligible California QREs). Furthermore, pursuant to Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-6(b) and (i) and Procter & Gamble Co. v. United States, 733 F. Supp. 2d 857 (S.D. Ohio 2010), any intercompany R&D service payments between Innovation Holdings Inc. and CaliTech LLC are disregarded, so only the underlying wages and supply expenses physically incurred in California are aggregated: $400,000 (Innovation Holdings Inc.) + $600,000 (CaliTech LLC) + $0 (Nevada Ops LLC) = $1,000,000 in Aggregate 2025 California QREs.

Step 2 — Computation of the 2025 California Group Credit Under the SB 711 ASC Method: The controlled group computes the 2025 California group credit under the Senate Bill 711 ASC method (R&TC Section 23609(h)(2)(A) and Section 17052.12(g)(2)(A)(i)). By electing the California Alternative Simplified Credit (which applies a 3 percent rate to current-year California QREs exceeding 50 percent of the prior three-year average California QREs) on Form FTB 3523, the group first determines its California ASC base amount by taking 50 percent of the $800,000 prior three-year average, which equals $400,000 (50% × $800,000). Subtracting the $400,000 ASC base amount from the $1,000,000 of current-year California QREs yields $600,000 in excess incremental California QREs ($1,000,000 − $400,000), which is then multiplied by the 3 percent statutory ASC rate to generate an $18,000 Aggregate 2025 California Group Credit ($600,000 × 3%).

Step 3 — Pro-Rata Allocation Across Controlled Group Members: The $18,000 California group credit is allocated pro rata across the controlled group members in accordance with post-ATRA IRC Section 41(f)(1) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-6(c) (T.D. 9832), strictly following each member's proportionate share of total California QREs and disregarding any hypothetical stand-alone base calculations. Because Innovation Holdings Inc. incurred $400,000 of the $1,000,000 aggregate California QREs (40.0 percent), it is allocated $7,200 of the group credit ($18,000 × 40.0%). Because CaliTech LLC incurred $600,000 of the $1,000,000 aggregate California QREs (60.0 percent), it is allocated $10,800 of the group credit ($18,000 × 60.0%). Because Nevada Ops LLC incurred $0 in California QREs (0.0 percent), it receives $0 of the California credit despite being a member of the federal controlled group.

body.text: Each eligible California entity reports its allocated credit share ($7,200 for Innovation Holdings Inc. and $10,800 for CaliTech LLC) on its respective Form FTB 3523.
Technological Compliance Systems and Audit Substantiation

The convergence of federal intercompany elimination rules under IRC Section 41(f) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-6(i), strict state geographic apportionment mandates under California R&TC Section 23609(c)(2) and Massachusetts 830 CMR 63.38M.1(4), and the granular project-level substantiation standards enforced in Appeal of First Solar, Inc. (2023-OTA-532P), Appeal of Electronic Data Systems Corporation & Subsidiaries (2023-OTA-540), and Appeal of Abramson, et al. (2024-OTA-636) exposes retrospective, spreadsheet-based R&D credit studies to acute audit disallowance risk. Traditional post-year-end reconstruction methods that rely on high-level cost-center estimates or uncorroborated retrospective interviews or surveys routinely fail to produce the chronological, business-component-specific documentation demanded by the FTB and OTA.

From a strictly technical tax compliance standpoint—independent of any specific proprietary vendor platform—the underlying legal takeaway established by federal and state authorities is unambiguous: multi-entity controlled groups must maintain automated or contemporaneous project-accounting controls capable of identifying all commonly controlled entities under the more-than-50-percent ownership test of IRC Section 41(f)(5) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.52-1, eliminating all internal intercompany billings and intra-group gross receipts under Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-6(i) and Procter & Gamble Co. v. United States, 733 F. Supp. 2d 857 (S.D. Ohio 2010), tracking the physical state location of every research employee hour, supply expenditure, and leased computer cluster, and tying those expenses directly to specific business components (and sub-components under the shrinking-back rule of Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(b)(2)) satisfying the four-part test of IRC Section 41(d).
Conclusion

IRC Section 41(f) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-6 establish a unified single-taxpayer architecture across commonly controlled corporations and unincorporated businesses, preventing intercompany transactions from inflating research tax credits and requiring pro-rata credit allocation strictly by current-year QRE share following the American Taxpayer Relief Act of 2012 and Treasury Decision 9832. When adopted at the state level under California R&TC Section 23609 and Section 17052.12 and Massachusetts M.G.L. Chapter 63, Section 38M (830 CMR 63.38M.1), this federal aggregation mandate operates alongside strict physical nexus rules that exclude out-of-state research expenditures, state-specific rate modifications such as California's 2025 adoption of the 3 percent and 1.3 percent Alternative Simplified Credit under Senate Bill 711, group-level credit utilization caps such as California's $5,000,000 limitation for 2024–2026 under R&TC Sections 23036.4 and 17039.4, entity-specific credit utilization restrictions under General Motors Corp. v. FTB, and rigorous project-by-project evidentiary burdens enforced by state tax tribunals.
